{{< include ../_provenance.qmd >}}

Questions beyond the clone labels: whether a clone's cells share a transcriptional state, whether a provirus acts on its neighbouring genes, how expression differs across replicates within a cluster, and which sites appear to share cells. Several of these are open rather than settled, and the section says which.

Part of the scarab integration-site analysis, which is four reports:
[method and parameters](../scarab-methods/scarab-methods.html) ·
[detections and confidence](../scarab-qc/scarab-qc.html) ·
[clones](../scarab-clones/scarab-clones.html) ·
[exploration](../scarab-exploration/scarab-exploration.html).

```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Shared across the four reports: the pipeline's output tables, the clone palette, the tube map and
# the parameter object. One file, so four reports cannot disagree about what they read or how a
# clone is coloured.
source("notebooks/integration-sites/_setup.R")

# The cell tables. The tar_read() is written out here, literally, rather than in _setup.R, because
# tar_knitr_deps() scans the .qmd and not the file it sources: a tar_read() inside _setup.R would
# leave the pipeline unaware that this report depends on the target at all.
#
# `is_cell_embedding` is a few megabytes - coordinates, cluster, replicate call and QC flag for all
# four processed objects - where the objects themselves are 2 GB each and cost ten minutes to read.
emb_all <- tar_read(is_cell_embedding)

# `embedding`, `labelled`, `embedding_raw`, `labelled_raw`, `hashtag_calls`, with the
# hashtag-file-against-object check that halts if one of them is stale.
list2env(build_cell_tables(emb_all), environment())
```

## Is any clone actually clustered? A permutation test

IS05's cells look clustered above, and that observation sat open in the handoff. Testing it is not
hard; getting the test *right* took three attempts, and two of them produced confident wrong answers
that are documented here rather than deleted.

**Not in UMAP space.** UMAP distances are not metric-faithful — the algorithm tears and stretches
neighbourhoods to make a readable picture — so clustering in the figure is not clustering in the
data. The test runs on the PCA coordinates the UMAP was built from, and the autocorrelation half on
the shared-nearest-neighbour graph Seurat already built. The UMAP above stays a picture.

**The null must be stratified by ANIMAL, not by tube.** Tubes are hashtag-multiplexed: Rx_4 holds
four mice. Every site in this dataset is mono-replicate by construction — that is what makes the
hashtag a clonality control in the first place — and the same fact means **every clone is perfectly
confounded with its animal**. No tube-level stratum can separate them.

**And by depth**, because labelled cells are systematically deeper than unlabelled ones (HSC median
4,725 genes against 3,728) — a junction read needs depth to be seen at all. Depth enters as a decile
*within* the stratum, so a permuted draw matches the observed set's animal, tube and depth profile.

**And the ranking statistic subtracts the null before dividing by detection:**

$$\text{excess per detection} = \frac{\text{enrichment} - \text{null}}{\text{detection}}$$

The signal scales with detection — each clonemate is seen with probability *d* — while the null is
drawn from the stratum pool and does not, so dividing the raw enrichment rescales a component that
needs no rescaling. The two orders disagree about which site ranks first; the comparison is printed
below the table.

```{r clustering-test}
#| cache: false
# Everything this report needs from the 2 GB HSC object, as four small targets: the PCA coordinates
# and metadata (is_cell_embedding, read in setup), the SNN graph, the loadings, and the counts.
# Reading the object itself took ten minutes and ~24 GB three times over in this report alone.
hsc_md  <- emb_all |> dplyr::filter(panel == "HSC", stage == "post-QC", pass_cell)
pcs_h   <- as.matrix(dplyr::select(hsc_md, dplyr::num_range("PC_", 1:30)))
cells_h <- hsc_md$cell
rownames(pcs_h) <- cells_h
tube_h  <- as.character(hsc_md$tube)
nfeat_h <- hsc_md$nFeature_RNA
clus_h  <- as.character(hsc_md$`sNN_pca.SCT_30_res.0.5`)
graph_h <- tar_read(is_hsc_graph)
# The PCA's variable features, to ask below whether the cis artefact can reach the statistic at all.
# From the loadings, not VariableFeatures(), which can be re-set after the PCA was run.
vf_h    <- rownames(tar_read(is_hsc_loadings))

# The graph is subset to pass_cell in _targets.R and the table is filtered on it here: two separate
# operations on two separate targets. Moran's I below indexes the graph POSITIONALLY by each cell's
# place in cells_h, so a disagreement about order would compute the autocorrelation on the wrong
# cells and still return a perfectly plausible number.
#
# So the graph is reordered to cells_h by NAME rather than asserted to match it. An earlier version
# asserted identical() and halted the render - which is the right failure, but the wrong remedy: the
# two orders agreeing is a property of how _targets.R happens to build them, and nothing downstream
# should depend on that holding. Subsetting by name makes the alignment true by construction, and
# the set check below is then the only thing that has to hold.
# Reported rather than asserted bare: a failed stopifnot() here printed only "is not TRUE", which
# does not distinguish a genuine cell-order mismatch from rownames() returning NULL because an S4
# method was not registered - and those need opposite remedies.
if (!setequal(rownames(graph_h), cells_h)) {
  stop("the SNN graph and the embedding disagree about which cells passed QC.\n",
       "  graph: ", nrow(graph_h), " rows, ",
       if (is.null(rownames(graph_h))) "NO rownames (is Matrix attached?)"
       else paste0(length(setdiff(rownames(graph_h), cells_h)), " not in the embedding"), "\n",
       "  embedding: ", length(cells_h), " cells, ",
       length(setdiff(cells_h, rownames(graph_h))), " not in the graph\n",
       "  Both come from mpn_processed_hsc_fullcc$pass_cell in _targets.R; one target is stale.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
stopifnot(ncol(pcs_h) == 30L, !anyNA(pcs_h))
graph_h <- graph_h[cells_h, cells_h]

akey_h <- paste0(assign$tube, "_", assign$barcode)
lab_h  <- assign$site_id[match(cells_h, akey_h)]
# A cell at more than one site belongs to neither here: it is a doublet or a multi-copy integrant,
# and either way its position is not evidence about one clone's state.
lab_h[cells_h %in% akey_h[assign$n_sites_in_cell > 1L]] <- NA
# `replicate` (B0301..B0304), not `call` (TotalSeq-B0301..): the short form is what
# replicate_confinement() and orphan_evidence.csv use, and two spellings of one animal in a single
# report is how a join silently returns nothing.
rep_h <- hashtag_calls$replicate[match(cells_h, hashtag_calls$cell)]

# Depth decile within whatever the stratum is, not within tube: once the stratum is tube x animal the
# pool is a tenth the size, and a tube-wide decile would pile a small animal into two bins.
decile_in <- function(groups, x = nfeat_h) {
  stats::ave(x, interaction(groups, drop = TRUE), FUN = function(v)
    as.integer(cut(rank(v, ties.method = "first"),
                   breaks = min(10, max(2, length(v) %/% 20)), labels = FALSE)))
}
strata_tube   <- paste(tube_h, decile_in(list(tube_h)), sep = ":")
strata_animal <- paste(tube_h, rep_h, decile_in(list(tube_h, rep_h)), sep = ":")

det_fit <- detr |>
  dplyr::filter(lambda_source == "fitted (ZTP)") |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, detection = detection_used)

clust_tube <- knn_site_clustering(pcs_h, lab_h, strata_tube, detection = det_fit,
                                  graph = graph_h, k = 30L, n_perm = 1000L, min_cells = 10L)
clust <- knn_site_clustering(pcs_h, lab_h, strata_animal, detection = det_fit,
                             graph = graph_h, k = 30L, n_perm = 1000L, min_cells = 10L)

animal_of <- function(ids) vapply(ids, function(s)
  names(sort(table(rep_h[!is.na(lab_h) & lab_h == s]), decreasing = TRUE))[1], character(1))

dplyr::left_join(
  clust |> dplyr::transmute(site_id, cells, animal = animal_of(site_id),
                            `null` = sprintf("%.4f", null_mean),
                            `z` = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                            `p` = ifelse(p_value <= 1 / (n_perm + 1),
                                         sprintf("< %.3f", 1 / (n_perm + 1)),
                                         sprintf("%.3f", p_value)),
                            `p Holm` = sprintf("%.3f", p_holm),
                            `Moran z` = sprintf("%.1f", morans_z),
                            `Moran p Holm` = sprintf("%.3f", morans_p_holm),
                            `excess / detection` = ifelse(is.na(excess_per_detection), "—",
                                                          sprintf("%.4f", excess_per_detection))),
  clust_tube |> dplyr::transmute(site_id, `z, tube-only null` = sprintf("%.1f", z)),
  by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::relocate(`z, tube-only null`, .after = animal) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlrrrrrrr")
```

`p Holm` corrects across the `r nrow(clust)` sites tested and is the pre-registered correction;
Bonferroni is not shown, because Holm dominates it uniformly and printing both would hand the reader
a choice at the one site where they differ. **`excess / detection` is `—` for IS10**, which has no
fitted λ (its truncated mean is 1.09, where the ZTP is degenerate), **so the two sites that clear the
test cannot be ranked against each other.** The plausible direction is worth stating: IS10's
molecules per cell are low, so its detection is probably low, and a small divisor would put its
adjusted excess *above* IS05's rather than below.

```{r clustering-readout}
#| echo: false
surv <- clust$site_id[clust$p_holm < 0.05]
cmp  <- clust |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(detection)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, plain = enrichment / detection, subtracted = excess_per_detection)
# HOLM on both sides, not raw p. Holm is the pre-registered correction, so "significant" has to
# mean the same thing in the prose as in the table - an earlier version filtered on raw p and so
# counted IS03 (animal-null raw p = 0.049, Holm 0.34) as surviving, which it does not.
lost <- clust_tube |> dplyr::filter(p_holm < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::anti_join(dplyr::filter(clust, p_holm < 0.05), by = "site_id") |> dplyr::pull(site_id)
never <- clust_tube |> dplyr::filter(p_holm >= 0.05, p_value < 0.05) |> dplyr::pull(site_id)
is02 <- clust[clust$site_id == "IS02", ]
```

**`r paste(sort(surv), collapse = " and ")` clear the test, and the animal stratum is what removed
the rest.** Compare the two *z* columns: the survivors fall by roughly half and stay at the
permutation floor, while every other site drops below significance. Two counts, because they say
different things. Corrected, **`r paste(lost, collapse = ", ")`** is what the animal stratum removes
— significant under the tube-only null at Holm
`r sprintf("%.3f", clust_tube$p_holm[clust_tube$site_id %in% lost][1])`, and
`r sprintf("%.2f", clust$p_holm[clust$site_id %in% lost][1])` once the null draws from its own
animal. Uncorrected, `r paste(never, collapse = " and ")` would have been reported too, at raw
*p* < 0.05 under the tube null; they never clear Holm under either.

**Multiplicity alone would not have caught `r lost[1]`** — its tube-null Holm value is
`r sprintf("%.3f", clust_tube$p_holm[clust_tube$site_id %in% lost][1])`, which survives at 0.05, and
Bonferroni's would not have either. The stratification did, and that is the useful finding here: the
correction a reader would reach for first is not the one that mattered.

On the statistic: the plain ratio ranks **`r cmp$site_id[which.max(cmp$plain)]`** first, the
null-subtracted form ranks **`r cmp$site_id[which.max(cmp$subtracted)]`** first. They are not
interchangeable and only the second is defensible.

IS02 is worth naming separately: the largest clone in the dataset, `r is02$cells` HSC cells, sits at
*z* = `r sprintf("%.1f", is02$z)` — indistinguishable from cells drawn from its own animal at matched
depth. That is a fact about IS02, not a result about clone size in general; one large unconfined clone
measured once is n = 1 for any claim about a relationship.

### Is the animal effect itself the explanation? The test that cannot answer it

Both survivors are B0304. The obvious worry is that B0304 cells are transcriptionally distinct as a
group, so anything drawn from them looks confined. Measured directly, with no clone label at all —
B0304 membership against a tube- and depth-matched draw from every animal:

```{r b0304-whole}
#| cache: false
lab_anim <- ifelse(!is.na(rep_h) & rep_h == "B0304", "B0304", NA_character_)
b0304_whole <- knn_site_clustering(pcs_h, lab_anim, strata_tube, graph = graph_h,
                                   k = 30L, n_perm = 1000L, min_cells = 50L)
# `relative` is computed BEFORE the formatted columns, and the formatted ones are given new names.
# Assigning `enrichment = sprintf(...)` and then dividing by `enrichment` in a later argument of the
# same transmute() divides by a character string - dplyr evaluates the arguments in order and the
# second one sees the first one's result. It is a parse-clean runtime error, which is the worst kind
# to put in a 25-minute render.
b0304_whole |>
  dplyr::transmute(`cells` = cells,
                   `share of panel` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cells / nrow(pcs_h)),
                   `relative` = sprintf("%.2f×", enrichment / null_mean),
                   `enrichment` = sprintf("%.3f", enrichment),
                   `null` = sprintf("%.3f", null_mean),
                   `z` = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                   `p` = sprintf("< %.3f", 1 / (n_perm + 1))) |>
  dplyr::relocate(`relative`, .after = `null`) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**B0304 is enriched for itself, strongly — and this does not bear on the clone findings, which is
worth spelling out because it looks as though it should.** The animal-stratified null *already*
draws from B0304, so if B0304 clusters as a group, every permuted draw lands in the same
B0304-dense regions and the null rises to meet it. That is exactly what was observed: IS05's null
went from 0.0018 under the tube stratum to 0.0048 under the animal stratum, a 2.7× rise. **The
animal effect is absorbed into the null by construction**, so measuring it again outside the null
confirms the original error without touching the corrected result.

Two further reasons not to read this table as a demotion. The effect is modest in relative terms —
`r sprintf("%.2f×", b0304_whole$enrichment / b0304_whole$null_mean)` against IS05's
`r sprintf("%.2f×", clust$enrichment[clust$site_id == "IS05"] / clust$null_mean[clust$site_id == "IS05"])`
— and at `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * b0304_whole$cells / nrow(pcs_h))` of the panel the statistic is
in a saturated regime where it is not comparable to a 48-cell clone anyway.

What *would* invalidate the clone findings is B0304 sub-structure that a clone's cells
disproportionately occupy. That is a different test, and it is the next one.

### The shared cluster, and the finding it removes

IS05's and IS10's neighbourhoods cross-enrich, and both clones over-occupy one transcriptional
cluster. If that cluster *is* their enrichment, neither result is about a clone. Re-run each site's
test with the shared cluster's cells removed from both the member set and the null pool:

```{r shared-cluster}
#| cache: false
i5_h  <- which(lab_h == "IS05"); i10_h <- which(lab_h == "IS10")
shared_clus <- names(which.max(table(clus_h[c(i5_h, i10_h)])))
sub_h  <- clus_h != shared_clus
clust_nosh <- knn_site_clustering(
  pcs_h[sub_h, , drop = FALSE], lab_h[sub_h],
  paste(tube_h[sub_h], rep_h[sub_h],
        decile_in(list(tube_h[sub_h], rep_h[sub_h]), nfeat_h[sub_h]), sep = ":"),
  detection = det_fit, graph = graph_h[sub_h, sub_h],
  k = 30L, n_perm = 1000L, min_cells = 10L)

dplyr::inner_join(
  clust |> dplyr::transmute(site_id, `cells, all` = cells, `z, all` = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                            `p Holm, all` = sprintf("%.3f", p_holm)),
  clust_nosh |> dplyr::transmute(site_id, `cells, excl.` = cells,
                                 `z, excl.` = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                                 `p Holm, excl.` = sprintf("%.3f", p_holm),
                                 `Moran z, excl.` = sprintf("%.1f", morans_z)),
  by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(as.numeric(`p Holm, excl.`)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

```{r shared-readout}
#| echo: false
zz <- function(tb, s) tb$z[tb$site_id == s]
hh <- function(tb, s) tb$p_holm[tb$site_id == s]
```

**IS05 survives and IS10 collapses.** Excluding cluster `r shared_clus` costs IS05 twenty of its
forty-eight cells and it still clears at *z* = `r sprintf("%.1f", zz(clust_nosh, "IS05"))`, Holm
`r sprintf("%.3f", hh(clust_nosh, "IS05"))`. IS10 goes from *z* =
`r sprintf("%.1f", zz(clust, "IS10"))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", zz(clust_nosh, "IS10"))`, Holm
`r sprintf("%.2f", hh(clust_nosh, "IS10"))` — **its enrichment was the shared cluster.** IS10 is
demoted: it is not an independent instance of clonal confinement, and the two-sites-one-mouse worry
resolves by one of them not being a finding.

So **there is one surviving result, not two**: IS05's cells are transcriptionally confined beyond
what its animal, its tube, its depth and the shared B0304 state account for. It is the
best-controlled claim in this report and it rests on 28 cells after the exclusion, which is the
honest denominator for it.

### The *cis* artefact: measured, subtracted, and not fully removable

A junction read is a read-through transcript overlapping the host gene, so at an intragenic
same-sense site — what `cis_confound` marks — the junction molecules are counted as host-gene UMIs
in exactly the cells carrying that site. Those cells then differ transcriptionally at that gene for a
purely technical reason. Three things have to be separated: whether the inflation exists, whether it
can reach the clustering statistic, and whether it can be removed.

```{r cis-artefact}
#| cache: false
cis_sites <- c("IS10", "IS11", "IS04", "IS03", "IS02", "IS01")
host_genes <- sites$gene[match(cis_sites, sites$site_id)]
# Genes within 1 Mb of IS10, for the window scan further down, read from the same GTF the pipeline
# annotates with so the two cannot disagree about what a gene is.
is10_row <- sites[sites$site_id == "IS10", ]
gtf_genes <- rtracklayer::import(gtf_path, format = "gtf", feature.type = "gene")
win_gr <- gtf_genes[as.character(GenomicRanges::seqnames(gtf_genes)) == is10_row$chrom[1] &
                      abs((GenomicRanges::start(gtf_genes) +
                             GenomicRanges::end(gtf_genes)) / 2 - is10_row$pos[1]) <= 1e6]
win_genes <- unique(stats::na.omit(win_gr$gene_name))
# is_hsc_counts is the RNA assay's counts, already subset to the cells that pass QC, so the only
# subsetting left here is to the genes this chunk asks about. Read and dropped rather than held: the
# full matrix is wanted again much further down, and holding it across everything between would be
# the one large object this report was split up to avoid.
cnt_all <- tar_read(is_hsc_counts)
# Reordered by name, for the reason given at the graph above: every per-cell vector in this chunk is
# indexed positionally against cells_h.
stopifnot(setequal(colnames(cnt_all), cells_h))
want_g  <- intersect(unique(c(host_genes, win_genes, "Klf6")), rownames(cnt_all))
cnt_h   <- as.matrix(cnt_all[want_g, cells_h, drop = FALSE])
tot_h   <- hsc_md$nCount_RNA
rm(cnt_all); invisible(gc(verbose = FALSE))

# Subtract a site's junction UMIs from its own host gene's counts, at two strengths. `umis_genomic`
# is the channel whose reads carry 120-140 bases of host and so are the ones Cell Ranger would count
# to the gene; `molecules` is every junction UMI at that cell and site, which over-corrects.
#
# AND ONLY AT SAME-SENSE SITES, which the first version of this got wrong in a way that manufactured
# the result below. A read-through transcript is counted as host-gene expression only when it runs
# in the gene's own direction; at an antisense site it is not counted there at all. Subtracting
# regardless therefore deletes real expression from exactly the cells being tested, and it shows: at
# IS02 the "correction" drove Ddx10 from -0.27 to -0.74 to -1.22 as more was taken away, monotone in
# how much was subtracted. That is the signature of over-correction, not of a stronger effect, and it
# was about to be written up as the headline finding.
#
# So the correct value for a site is the fully subtracted one if it is same-sense and the unadjusted
# one if it is antisense. `orientation_corrected()` below picks per site rather than leaving a reader
# to notice which column to read.
strip_junctions <- function(m, column, same_sense_only = TRUE) {
  removed <- 0L
  same <- sites$site_id[isTRUE_vec(sites$cis_confound)]
  for (r in seq_len(nrow(assign))) {
    if (same_sense_only && !assign$site_id[r] %in% same) next
    hg <- sites$gene[match(assign$site_id[r], sites$site_id)]
    if (is.na(hg) || !(hg %in% rownames(m))) next
    j <- match(paste0(assign$tube[r], "_", assign$barcode[r]), cells_h)
    if (is.na(j)) next
    u <- assign[[column]][r]
    if (is.na(u) || u == 0L) next
    removed <- removed + min(m[hg, j], u)
    m[hg, j] <- max(0, m[hg, j] - u)
  }
  attr(m, "removed") <- removed
  m
}
cnt_gen <- strip_junctions(cnt_h, "umis_genomic")
cnt_all <- strip_junctions(cnt_h, "molecules")

set.seed(20261119L)
# No cluster matching from here on. Cluster membership is DOWNSTREAM of the hypothesis - if a
# provirus alters its neighbourhood's expression and that is why the cells sit together, the cluster
# is the mediator - so matching on it conditions on the mediator and bounds only the direct effect.
host_scan <- function(m, tag) dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(cis_sites), function(k) {
  if (!(host_genes[k] %in% rownames(m))) return(NULL)
  matched_expression_test(host_genes[k], cis_sites[k], m, tot_h, lab_h, rep_h, tube_h,
                          rep("all", length(clus_h)), nfeat_h)
})) |> dplyr::mutate(adjustment = tag)

cis_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  host_scan(cnt_h,  "none"),
  host_scan(cnt_gen, "genome channel"),
  host_scan(cnt_all, "all junction UMIs"))

# The value to read per site: fully subtracted where subtraction is valid, unadjusted where it is
# not. Nothing else in this report should quote a single "corrected" column across all six sites.
orientation_corrected <- function() {
  same <- sites$site_id[isTRUE_vec(sites$cis_confound)]
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    cis_tbl |> dplyr::filter(adjustment == "all junction UMIs", site_id %in% same) |>
      dplyr::mutate(basis = "junction UMIs subtracted"),
    cis_tbl |> dplyr::filter(adjustment == "none", !site_id %in% same) |>
      dplyr::mutate(basis = "unadjusted (subtraction invalid)"))
}

cis_tbl |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, `host gene` = gene, adjustment,
                   `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                   `% detected` = sprintf("%.0f%% vs %.0f%%", 100 * pct_site, 100 * pct_ctl),
                   p = sprintf("%.1g", p_value),
                   `in the PCA?` = ifelse(gene %in% vf_h, "**yes**", "no")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(site_id, `host gene`, `in the PCA?`),
                     names_from = adjustment,
                     values_from = c(`log2 FC`, p)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lllrrrrrr")
```

**The inflation is real and large**, up to +2.5 log₂ at IS10's host gene with 96% of its cells
detected against 18% of matched controls. **It cannot reach the clustering statistic**, and the
reason is one column: the PCA is built on 3,000 variable features, and the inflated host genes of the
sites that mattered are not among them. An inflated gene absent from the PCA cannot load a component.
Checking membership is cheaper and more direct than rebuilding the counts matrix, and it is the check
to run first.

### Orientation predicts the sign, which says what the effect is

Two of the six host genes move the *other* way, and that looked like an oddity until the insertions'
orientations were put beside them. It is not an oddity; it is the mechanism.

```{r cis-orientation}
#| cache: false
orient <- sites |>
  dplyr::filter(site_id %in% cis_sites) |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, gene, site = strand, host = gene_strand,
                   orientation = ifelse(strand == gene_strand, "same sense", "**antisense**"),
                   cis_confound) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    orientation_corrected() |> dplyr::transmute(site_id, log2fc, p_value, basis),
    by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(log2fc))

orient |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, `host gene` = gene, orientation,
                   `cis_confound` = cis_confound,
                   `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                   p = sprintf("%.1g", p_value),
                   `corrected how` = basis) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lllrrrl")
```

```{r cis-orientation-test}
#| echo: false
tb <- table(sign(orient$log2fc), grepl("antisense", orient$orientation))
ft <- stats::fisher.test(tb)
n_anti <- sum(grepl("antisense", orient$orientation))
```

**Every same-sense site goes up and every antisense site goes down — `r nrow(orient)` of
`r nrow(orient)`, and the split holds on the unadjusted counts too** (+2.20, +2.40, +1.27, +1.00
against −0.27, −0.18), which matters because it means the pattern is not produced by the correction. With `r nrow(orient) - n_anti` same-sense and `r n_anti` antisense sites, the
chance of the negatives falling exactly on the antisense pair is
1/`r choose(nrow(orient), n_anti)` = `r sprintf("%.3f", ft$p.value)`. **Suggestive, not significant**,
and on six sites it cannot be more than that — but the direction is what a mechanism predicts rather
than what noise predicts, and the mechanism is specific:

- **Same-sense.** A read-through transcript continues in the host gene's own direction, so Cell
  Ranger counts it as that gene's expression. The elevation *is* the artefact, by construction — and
  `cis_confound`, derived from annotation alone and with no knowledge of any of this, flags exactly
  these four.
- **Antisense.** The read-through runs against the gene, so it cannot be counted to it. No inflation
  is possible, and the decrease that remains is uncontaminated.

**This changes the reading of the residual.** Subtracting every extractable junction UMI left 0.8–2.4
log₂ at IS10, IS11 and IS03 and that was recorded as not separable from a real *cis* effect. It is
now separable in one direction: the residual occurs **only at same-sense sites**, which is where the
artefact lives and nowhere else. A genuine *cis* effect has no reason to track orientation that
perfectly — a provirus can perturb a neighbouring gene whichever way it points. So incomplete
correction is now the better-supported reading, and the three "surviving" elevations should not be
quoted as *cis* effects.

**The antisense decrease is much weaker than the uncorrected columns suggest, and that is a
correction this report had to make to itself.** Subtracting junction UMIs at an antisense site
deletes expression that was never added, so the "fully corrected" value there is over-corrected. The
three-level table above shows the damage directly: at IS02 the subtraction drove *Ddx10* from
**−0.27** to −0.74 to −0.92 as more was taken away — monotone in how much was removed, which is the
signature of over-correction rather than of a stronger effect.

```{r antisense-readout}
#| echo: false
# Computed in a chunk, not inline. The first version of this was a single inline `r {...}` holding
# an assignment, a paste() and three subsets - and it was missing its closing brace, which no chunk
# checker caught because inline expressions are not chunks. It cost a 25-minute render. Inline code
# in this report should reference a value, not build one.
anti <- orientation_corrected() |>
  dplyr::filter(basis != "junction UMIs subtracted")
anti_txt <- paste(sprintf("*%s* %+.2f (*p* = %.2g)", anti$gene, anti$log2fc, anti$p_value),
                  collapse = " and ")
```

Read on the basis that is valid for each site, the antisense pair is `r anti_txt`.

So **one small decrease and one that is not significant**, not two clean effects. Antisense insertion
reducing a gene's expression is an ordinary mechanism and these are the only two measurements here
the artefact cannot inflate — but two sites, one of them null, is not a result, and both are B0303's
largest clones so a shared state effect is not excluded either.

**And it is only partly removable.** Subtracting the genome channel's junction UMIs
(`r attr(cnt_gen, "removed")` of them) shrinks every effect; subtracting *all* junction UMIs
(`r attr(cnt_all, "removed")`) removes **IS04's entirely** — from +1.33 to +0.55 at *p* = 0.9 — while
IS10's, IS11's and IS03's survive at 1–2.4 log₂ and *p* < 10⁻⁶. Either those three are genuine *cis*
effects on the host gene, or the subtraction is still incomplete: the clip table holds only molecules
whose soft clip was long enough to extract, and a read-through whose clip fell below that threshold
is counted by Cell Ranger and not subtracted here. **This data cannot separate the two**, because the
artefact and the label are the same event — every cell of a site is, by definition, a cell that
yielded a junction molecule there, so there is no uncontaminated within-site comparison to make.

One route is closed for good, though: junction UMIs cannot move anything through library size.
`r attr(cnt_all, "removed")` UMIs against a median `nCount_RNA` of
`r scales::comma(round(stats::median(tot_h)))` is under 0.01% of the total, so every *other* gene is
untouched.

This also retires a claim made here earlier. The *cis*-loading screen flagged the two sites carrying
`cis_confound = TRUE` and cleared the one flagged `FALSE`, which was described as independent
validation of the annotation. It is agreement over three sites, which is evidence of nothing, and
IS04 — one of the two it flagged — turns out to have no host-gene effect at all once the artefact is
subtracted. The claim is withdrawn.

### *Klf6*, and the window around IS10

IS10 sits 239 kb from *Klf6*, a haematopoietic transcription factor, in an MPN-to-AML model — within
enhancer-activation range, where the *LMO2* events in the X-SCID trials worked. *Klf6* loaded three of
IS10's five most discriminating PCs. But a loading is a screen, not a test: PCs are global, so a gene
loading a discriminating component varies across the dataset, which is not the same as differing in
IS10's cells. And *Klf6* is immune to the artefact above, because IS10's junction reads land in its
own host gene 239 kb away.

```{r klf6-window}
#| cache: false
set.seed(20261119L)
win_scan <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(intersect(win_genes, rownames(cnt_all)), function(gg)
  matched_expression_test(gg, "IS10", cnt_all, tot_h, lab_h, rep_h, tube_h,
                          rep("all", length(clus_h)), nfeat_h))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(p_holm = stats::p.adjust(p_value, "holm")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(p_value)
ctrl <- matched_expression_test("Klf6", "IS05", cnt_all, tot_h, lab_h, rep_h, tube_h,
                                rep("all", length(clus_h)), nfeat_h)

dplyr::bind_rows(win_scan, dplyr::mutate(ctrl, gene = "Klf6 (IS05, off-chromosome control)")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(gene, `cells / controls` = sprintf("%d / %d", n_site, n_ctl),
                   `mean CPM` = sprintf("%.2f vs %.2f", mean_site, mean_ctl),
                   `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                   p = sprintf("%.2g", p_value),
                   `p Holm` = ifelse(is.na(p_holm), "—", sprintf("%.3f", p_holm))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

```{r klf6-readout}
#| echo: false
kl <- win_scan[win_scan$gene == "Klf6", ]
hit <- win_scan |> dplyr::filter(p_holm < 0.05, abs(log2fc) > 0.3)
```

***Klf6* does not clear the bar.** +`r sprintf("%.2f", kl$log2fc)` log₂ at raw
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", kl$p_value)`, which is Holm `r sprintf("%.2f", kl$p_holm)` across the
`r nrow(win_scan)` genes in the window — and the effect sits at the 0.3 log₂ threshold rather than
above it. The off-chromosome control is `r sprintf("%+.2f", ctrl$log2fc)` at
*p* = `r sprintf("%.2f", ctrl$p_value)`, so **the design's resolution is roughly 0.2–0.3 log₂, and
the honest statement is that it resolves nothing below that** — not that the effect is +0.26.

*A note on the earlier version of this test.* It matched controls on transcriptional cluster as well,
and returned +0.09 at *p* = 0.36 with the control at −0.33, *p* = 0.06. Cluster is the mediator here:
if the provirus alters *Klf6* and that is why the cells sit together, matching on cluster conditions
on the very thing being tested, bounding only the effect *net of state*. Dropping it both raised the
estimate and cleaned up the control, which is the signature of having conditioned on a mediator.

**The window scan finds one Holm-significant gene and it is the artefact.**
`r if (nrow(hit)) paste0("*", hit$gene[1], "*, at ", sprintf("%+.2f", hit$log2fc[1]), " log2") else "none"`
— IS10's own host gene, which the section above shows cannot be cleanly separated from junction-read
contamination. So nothing in ±1 Mb is a clean candidate. The scan is also thin: of
`r length(win_genes)` annotated genes in the window only `r nrow(win_scan)` are in the expression
matrix at all, the rest being undetected in this tissue.

**None of which now needs to explain anything**, because IS10's confinement did not survive the
shared-cluster test. The *cis* question at IS10 is closed as unsupported rather than open: no gene in
reach shows a clean effect, and there is no longer a confinement for one to account for. A targeted
measurement — *Klf6* by qPCR or 4C in sorted IS10 cells — would be the way to pursue it, and is
outside what this data can do.


### What makes IS05's cells sit together

With IS10 demoted, IS05 is the one surviving confinement, and until now nothing had been asked about
its locus — it appeared in the section above only as the *off-chromosome control* for the IS10
*Klf6* test. It is also the cleanest case available: `cis_confound = FALSE`, and its host gene is
absent from the PCA's variable features, so the junction-read artefact cannot reach it.

Two questions, in order. Is anything differentially expressed in its cells at all, and is any of it
near the integration site?

```{r is05-de}
#| cache: false
# The FULL counts matrix, not cnt_h: that one holds only the host genes and the IS10 window, and an
# unbiased scan needs every gene. Kept sparse - matched_de() does its arithmetic on Matrix columns,
# and densifying 11,000 x 50,000 here would cost gigabytes for no gain.
cnt_full <- tar_read(is_hsc_counts)[, cells_h, drop = FALSE]   # aligned by name; see above

set.seed(20261119L)
# Controls matched on animal, tube and depth but NOT cluster. Cluster is the mediator: if the clone
# occupies a transcriptional state, matching on it conditions on the thing being measured.
is05_de <- matched_de("IS05", cnt_full, tot_h, lab_h, rep_h, tube_h,
                      cluster = NULL, depth = nfeat_h)
is05_de |>
  dplyr::filter(p_holm < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::transmute(gene, `mean CPM` = sprintf("%.2f vs %.2f", mean_site, mean_ctl),
                   `% detected` = sprintf("%.0f%% vs %.0f%%", 100 * pct_site, 100 * pct_ctl),
                   `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                   p = sprintf("%.1g", p_value), `p Holm` = sprintf("%.1g", p_holm)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

**`r sum(is05_de$p_holm < 0.05)` genes, out of `r scales::comma(is05_de$n_tested[1])` tested.** The
up-regulated set — *Vwf*, *Clu*, *Clec11a*, *Selenom*, *Neo1* — is the **Vwf⁺ platelet-biased
long-term HSC** programme, which is a coherent thing for a clone to occupy in a
myeloproliferative model rather than a grab-bag of unrelated genes.

```{r is05-cis}
#| cache: false
is05_row <- sites[sites$site_id == "IS05", ]
win05 <- gtf_genes[as.character(GenomicRanges::seqnames(gtf_genes)) == is05_row$chrom[1] &
                     abs((GenomicRanges::start(gtf_genes) +
                            GenomicRanges::end(gtf_genes)) / 2 - is05_row$pos[1]) <= 1e6]
win05_genes <- unique(stats::na.omit(win05$gene_name))
is05_de |>
  dplyr::filter(gene %in% win05_genes) |>
  dplyr::mutate(p_holm_window = stats::p.adjust(p_value, "holm")) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 6) |>
  dplyr::transmute(gene, `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                   p = sprintf("%.3f", p_value),
                   `p Holm, within window` = sprintf("%.2f", p_holm_window)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

**Nothing in ±1 Mb.** Of `r length(win05_genes)` annotated genes in the window,
`r sum(win05_genes %in% is05_de$gene)` are expressed enough to test and the best of them does not
survive correction within the window. So IS05's confinement is **not *cis***, which agrees with its
`cis_confound = FALSE` flag arrived at from annotation alone.

```{r is05-mediation}
#| cache: false
set.seed(20261119L)
# The same test WITH cluster matched. A gene that loses significance here was explained by which
# cluster the cells are in; one that survives differs within the state as well.
is05_de_cl <- matched_de("IS05", cnt_full, tot_h, lab_h, rep_h, tube_h,
                         cluster = clus_h, depth = nfeat_h)
dplyr::inner_join(
  dplyr::filter(is05_de, p_holm < 0.05) |>
    dplyr::transmute(gene, `log2 FC` = sprintf("%+.2f", log2fc),
                     `p Holm, cluster free` = sprintf("%.1g", p_holm)),
  is05_de_cl |> dplyr::transmute(gene, holm_cl = p_holm),
  by = "gene") |>
  dplyr::mutate(`p Holm, cluster matched` = sprintf("%.2g", holm_cl),
                `survives?` = ifelse(holm_cl < 0.05, "**within state**",
                                     "explained by state")) |>
  dplyr::select(-holm_cl) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrl")
```

```{r is05-mediation-readout}
#| echo: false
surv05 <- is05_de_cl$gene[is05_de_cl$p_holm < 0.05 &
                            is05_de_cl$gene %in% is05_de$gene[is05_de$p_holm < 0.05]]
i5_cl <- table(clus_h[lab_h == "IS05" & !is.na(lab_h)])
bg_cl <- table(clus_h[!is.na(rep_h) & rep_h == "B0304" & tube_h == "Rx_4"])
top_cl <- names(which.max(i5_cl))
```

**The confinement is part cell-state and part within-state, and the split is the answer.**
`r length(surv05)` of the `r sum(is05_de$p_holm < 0.05)` genes survive matching on cluster; the rest
are explained by *which* cluster IS05's cells are in. And they are concentrated in one:
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(i5_cl) / sum(i5_cl))` of IS05's cells sit in cluster `r top_cl`
against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bg_cl[top_cl] / sum(bg_cl))` of its animal's background.

So the open question closes as follows. **IS05's cells cluster because the clone occupies a Vwf⁺ HSC
state, disproportionately but not exclusively, and because within that state it is still
*Vwf*-higher than its neighbours.** What this does *not* establish is direction of causation: a
provirus that pushed its cell into that state and a clone that happened to arise in such a cell
predict the same picture, and the *cis* result rules out only the simplest version of the first.

**One gene does not fit and is reported rather than explained.** *Rnf17* is the strongest hit by a
wide margin — `r sprintf("%+.1f", is05_de$log2fc[is05_de$gene == "Rnf17"])` log₂,
detected in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * is05_de$pct_site[is05_de$gene == "Rnf17"])` of IS05's cells
and **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * is05_de$pct_ctl[is05_de$gene == "Rnf17"])`** of controls — and it is
a piRNA-pathway gene with no known haematopoietic role. It is on a different chromosome from IS05, so
it is not *cis*, and its *p* is unchanged by cluster matching, so it is not a state effect. A gene
absent from 240 matched cells and present in a quarter of a clone's is either a real clone-specific
expression or an artefact this report has not identified; it needs a targeted look rather than a
sentence here.


## Cells carrying more than one site

```{r ambiguous}
amb <- labelled %>%
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(tube, barcode, n_sites_in_cell)

dplyr::count(amb, n_sites_in_cell, name = "cells") %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

These are flagged rather than resolved, deliberately. A cell showing two strong junctions is either a
genuine multi-copy integrant or a doublet, and no single cell tells you which. Treating them as
multi-copy clones would inflate clone counts; dropping them would deflate them. They are marked
`ambiguous` so downstream analyses can make that choice explicitly.

Across all cells the two explanations make different predictions, so the comparison below is worth
making — but the denominator decides the answer, and the obvious choice for it is wrong.

Taking `n` to be the number of *labelled* barcodes builds the detection rate into the expectation
and all but guarantees the verdict "below chance". Under the same-clone hypothesis the right
denominator is the clone's **true size** `N`, which is far larger than the number of cells in which
a site was detected: cells showing both sites is then `|A| × |B| / N`. Inverting that is informative
in itself — 146 × 190 / 12 = 2,312 is the clone size in Rx_4 *if* IS01 and IS02 mark one clone, and
3,164 is the same figure for Rx_6, which are numbers to put next to the doublet explanation rather
than leave implicit.

The table therefore reports both denominators, and the conclusion follows the conservative one.

```{r cooccurrence}
cooccur <- function(tube_id) {
  d    <- dplyr::filter(assign, tube == tube_id)
  n    <- dplyr::n_distinct(d$barcode)
  sets <- split(d$barcode, droplevels(d$site_id))
  sets <- sets[lengths(sets) >= 3]
  ids  <- names(sets)
  if (length(ids) < 2) return(NULL)
  pairs <- utils::combn(ids, 2, simplify = FALSE)
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(pairs, function(p) {
    a <- unique(sets[[p[1]]]); b <- unique(sets[[p[2]]])
    obs <- length(intersect(a, b))
    dplyr::tibble(tube = tube_id, pair = paste(p, collapse = " + "),
                  cells_A = length(a), cells_B = length(b),
                  observed = obs,
                  # The denominator that builds in the detection rate, kept only for comparison.
                  exp_labelled = round(length(a) * length(b) / n, 1),
                  # Under the same-clone hypothesis, at a plausible true clone size.
                  exp_if_one_clone_2000 = round(length(a) * length(b) / 2000, 1),
                  # And the clone size that would be implied if the pair really were one clone.
                  N_implied = ifelse(obs > 0, round(length(a) * length(b) / obs), NA_integer_))
  }))
}

dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("Rx_4", "Rx_6"), cooccur)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(cells_A + cells_B)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "tp", pageLength = 8))
```

Against the labelled-cell denominator every informative pair falls below expectation, which on its
own settles nothing: that denominator builds the detection rate into the expectation, and the zeros
are shared by both hypotheses — same-clone predicts ≈0.1 for a 45 × 5 pair and disjoint clones
predict 0, so their agreement discriminates nothing.

### The control that does discriminate: pairs from different mice

The hashtag demultiplex supplies a control the earlier analysis did not use. Every site is
mono-replicate, so **two sites in different mice cannot share a cell.** Any co-occurrence between
them is a doublet, an ambient pick-up, or a mistake. Splitting the pairs that way turns the doublet
explanation from an assumption into a measurement.

```{r cooccurrence-by-mouse}
# Which mouse each site belongs to: the dominant hashtag class, 96-100% of every site's cells.
site_replicate <- labelled |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^TotalSeq-B03", as.character(replicate))) |>
  dplyr::count(site_id, replicate) |>
  dplyr::group_by(site_id) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id = as.character(site_id), mouse = sub("^TotalSeq-", "", replicate))

pair_class <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("Rx_4", "Rx_6"), cooccur)) |>
  tidyr::separate(pair, into = c("A", "B"), sep = " [+] ", remove = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::rename(site_replicate, A = site_id, mouseA = mouse), by = "A") |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::rename(site_replicate, B = site_id, mouseB = mouse), by = "B") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mouseA), !is.na(mouseB)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = ifelse(mouseA == mouseB, "same mouse", "different mice"))

pair_class |>
  dplyr::group_by(tube, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(pairs = dplyr::n(), observed = sum(observed),
                   `expected if independent` = round(sum(exp_labelled), 1),
                   `obs / exp` = round(sum(observed) / sum(exp_labelled), 4),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

A doublet process does not know which mouse a cell came from, so it would hit both classes at the
same rate. Apply the same-mouse rate to the cross-mouse pairs and it predicts **33.9** co-occurrences;
**one** was observed (Poisson *p* ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁴).

**The obvious objection to that, and why it does not hold here.** A droplet holding cells from two
mice carries two hashtags, which is exactly what a demultiplexer calls a doublet — so if such
droplets had been dropped before this test, cross-mouse pairs would have been stripped from the very
set the test runs on, along the exact axis of the comparison and in the direction of the conclusion.
That would be fatal. It is not what happened: **this test is run on every labelled barcode,
hashtag-multiplets included.** Of the 1,131 labelled cells in Rx_4 and Rx_6, 971 are called singlets,
**130 are called multiplets** and 30 have no call. Splitting the test by the demultiplexer's own
verdict shows where the one event lives (same minimum site size of three cells throughout, so the
first row is the table above pooled over both tubes):

| subset of barcodes | cells | cross-mouse obs / exp | same-mouse obs / exp |
|---|---|---|---|
| all labelled cells (what the test uses) | 1,131 | 1 / 263.5 | 26 / 202.1 |
| hashtag **singlets** only | 971 | 0 / 226.0 | 23 / 174.7 |
| hashtag **multiplets**, negatives, no call | 160 | 1 / 32.8 | 3 / 27.0 |

The single cross-mouse co-occurrence — Rx_4, IS02 + IS10, B0303 + B0304 — **is** a called multiplet,
precisely as a doublet should be: the demultiplexer caught it rather than hiding it. And in the
subset most enriched for doublets, cross-mouse co-occurrence is still **33-fold below independence**
rather than near it, while same-mouse co-occurrence in that same subset sits at the same ratio as
everywhere else. The depletion is not an artefact of demultiplexing.

**So doublets do not explain the co-occurrences, and the earlier claim that they could is withdrawn.**
Ambient goes with them: ambient RNA comes from the whole tube's soup, which carries every mouse's
clones in proportion to their abundance, so it too would produce cross-mouse pairs. One event in 263
expected is the measured ceiling on both mechanisms together. The reason both are so rare is worth
stating because it is not obvious: for a doublet to *show* two sites, **both** of its cells must be
detected, and detection is a few per cent per cell.

What is left is that sites **within one mouse share cells far above that floor**, which is what a
multi-copy founder looks like. Every one of the 26 co-occurrences is in B0303, and all six
co-occurring pairs are drawn from IS01, IS02, IS06 and IS08.

**Which expectation came from which model, because the two point opposite ways.** The 202.1 above is
`|A|·|B| / N_labelled`: the independence expectation *if every cell of every clone were detected*.
Same-mouse co-occurrence at 26 against that is running at an eighth of it — and read naively that
argues against sharing, since cells of a multi-copy founder carry both proviruses by construction.
It is not the right expectation. Under a shared founder the denominator is the clone's **true** size,
so the prediction is `|A|·|B| / N_true`, and 26 observed is then a statement about how much larger
`N_true` is than the detected count — the eight-fold shortfall *is* the detection rate. The
cross-mouse contrast is immune to this, because both classes use the same convention and the
comparison is between them, which is why the result rests on it.

### The discriminator that uses detection depth

Co-occurrence counts cannot separate "one clone, partly detected" from "two clones plus correlated
detection", because both are fitted by choosing a denominator. Detection *depth* can. If IS01 and
IS02 sit in one founder, every cell of it carries both and the only reason both are not seen is how
many junction molecules that cell yielded. So condition on that count:

```{r dose-response}
# Depth is DISTINCT MOLECULES per cell, taken from the clip table's one-row-per-molecule shape.
# It must not be umis_three + umis_genomic: that double-counts the 83 molecules seen in both
# channels and pushes single-molecule cells into the two-molecule stratum, where a cell cannot show
# two sites by construction - which deflates sharing exactly where the fraction is read off.
depth <- clip_tbl |>
  dplyr::semi_join(called_barcodes, by = c("tube", "barcode")) |>
  dplyr::filter(tube %in% c("Rx_4", "Rx_6")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(tube, barcode) |>
  dplyr::summarise(k = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    assign |>
      dplyr::filter(tube %in% c("Rx_4", "Rx_6")) |>
      dplyr::group_by(tube, barcode) |>
      dplyr::summarise(s = list(as.character(site_id)), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c("tube", "barcode"))

# p comes from the FITTED lambdas, not from each site's share of molecules across both sites' cells:
# that share includes the non-shared cells and so biases p.
lam <- stats::setNames(detect_tbl$lambda, detect_tbl$site_id)

depth_curve <- function(a, b, label) {
  p <- lam[[a]] / (lam[[a]] + lam[[b]])
  depth |>
    dplyr::mutate(hasA = purrr::map_lgl(s, ~ a %in% .x),
                  hasB = purrr::map_lgl(s, ~ b %in% .x)) |>
    dplyr::filter(hasA | hasB) |>
    dplyr::mutate(k = pmin(k, 4L)) |>
    dplyr::group_by(k) |>
    dplyr::summarise(cells = dplyr::n(), both = sum(hasA & hasB),
                     observed = mean(hasA & hasB), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(pair = label,
                  `if one clone` = 1 - p^k - (1 - p)^k)
}

dose <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  depth_curve("IS01", "IS02", "IS01 + IS02 — same mouse"),
  depth_curve("IS02", "IS04", "IS02 + IS04 — different mice"))

dose |>
  dplyr::transmute(pair, `molecules in the cell` = k, cells, both,
                   observed = round(observed, 3),
                   `if one clone` = round(`if one clone`, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r dose-plot}
#| fig-cap: "Sharing against detection depth. The same-mouse pair rises with the number of junction
#|   molecules a cell yielded; the cross-mouse control is flat at zero at every depth, including the
#|   deepest cells. The dashed line is what full sharing would predict from the fitted detection
#|   rates - the gap between it and the observed series bounds the sub-clone fraction."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

pair_pal <- c(`IS01 + IS02 — same mouse` = "#D55E00",
              `IS02 + IS04 — different mice` = "#0072B2")

ggplot(dose, aes(k, observed, colour = pair)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = `if one clone`), linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(size = cells), stroke = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pair_pal, name = NULL) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, breaks = c(10, 100, 500), name = "cells") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = c("1", "2", "3", "4+")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "junction molecules in the cell", y = "carrying both sites",
       title = "Sharing rises with depth for one pair and not the other") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

```{r dose-readout}
#| echo: false
# Read off the table above rather than typed. The prose here carried 0.105 and 0.493 for k = 2,
# which are 12/114 and a p from the superseded "share of molecules" definition - the depth variable
# was corrected to DISTINCT molecules and these numbers were not. 0.105 is the fingerprint of the
# old umis_three + umis_genomic denominator, which pushed single-molecule cells into k = 2.
ds <- dplyr::filter(dose, grepl("same mouse", pair))
at <- function(kk, col) ds[[col]][ds$k == kk]
frac <- function(kk) at(kk, "observed") / at(kk, "if one clone")
fish <- stats::fisher.test(matrix(c(
  at(2, "both"), at(2, "cells") - at(2, "both"),
  dose$both[dose$k == 2 & grepl("different", dose$pair)],
  dose$cells[dose$k == 2 & grepl("different", dose$pair)]), nrow = 2))
```

**There is a dose–response, and the matched control is flat at zero.** Sharing rises with detection
depth for the same-mouse pair — `r paste(sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ds$observed[order(ds$k)][1:3]), collapse = ", then ")`
— and stays at exactly zero for the cross-mouse pair at every depth. At matched depth `k = 2` the
contrast is `r at(2, "both")` of `r at(2, "cells")` against
`r dose$both[dose$k == 2 & grepl("different", dose$pair)]` of
`r dose$cells[dose$k == 2 & grepl("different", dose$pair)]`, Fisher exact
*p* = `r sprintf("%.5f", fish$p.value)`. Doublets and correlated detection do not produce a depth
gradient in one pair and a flat zero in another; partial detection of a shared founder does.

**But it reaches only part of what full sharing predicts**, and the fraction is not stable:
`r sprintf("%.2f against %.2f", at(2, "observed"), at(2, "if one clone"))` at `k = 2` — a ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", frac(2))` — and `r sprintf("%.2f against %.2f", at(3, "observed"), at(3, "if one clone"))`
at `k = 3`, a ratio of `r sprintf("%.2f", frac(3))`. **And at `k = 4` it falls back to
`r sprintf("%.2f", at(4, "observed"))` on `r at(4, "cells")` cells**, which a dose–response cannot
do and noise at that count easily can. So the honest reading is a sub-clone fraction somewhere
between a quarter and two-thirds, bounded by strata of 101, 16 and 9 cells — a double-insertion
sub-clone inside B0303 rather than a single founder carrying everything, with the *size* of the
sub-clone essentially unconstrained. An earlier draft of this paragraph quoted "a quarter to a
third" from the `k = 2` and `k = 3` strata under the superseded counting and stopped before `k = 4`.

That still explains the inconsistent implied sizes the pair-counting produced — IS01 + IS02 implying
2,312 cells against IS01 + IS06 implying 365 — which the previous draft could only record as a
caveat.

**One piece of internal consistency, worth stating because the hypothesis has little else.** IS03 is
a B0303 site with 130 cells and it appears in **none** of the 26 co-occurrences. Under the
sub-clone reading that is exactly right: IS03 is an independent clone in the same mouse. Under a
doublet mechanism its absence would be unexplained, since doublets do not know which sites travel
together.

### Testing the sub-clone on something other than co-occurrence

Everything above is one statistic read several ways. If a double-insertion sub-clone really exists
inside B0303, its cells are a coherent subpopulation and should look like one in data that the
co-occurrence test never touched: where they sit on the UMAP, and in what ratio they carry the two
proviruses. A real sub-clone predicts the sharing cells carry IS01 and IS02 at a balanced ratio and
occupy the same region as the single-site cells of their own clone; correlated detection predicts no
such structure, just the deepest cells of a mixed population.

```{r subclone-test}
#| fig-cap: "Cells carrying IS01, IS02 or both, on the HSC and MNC embeddings, with the within-cell
#|   molecule ratio for the sharing cells. A sub-clone predicts the both-sites cells sit with the
#|   single-site cells rather than apart, and carry the two proviruses at a balanced ratio."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2

share_class <- assign |>
  dplyr::filter(site_id %in% c("IS01", "IS02")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cell) |>
  dplyr::summarise(sites = paste(sort(unique(as.character(site_id))), collapse = "+"),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = dplyr::recode(sites, "IS01" = "IS01 only", "IS02" = "IS02 only",
                                      "IS01+IS02" = "both sites"))

share_pal <- c(`IS01 only` = "#0072B2", `IS02 only` = "#D55E00", `both sites` = "#009E73")

sub_umap <- dplyr::inner_join(share_class, embedding, by = "cell") |>
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell)

p_umap <- ggplot(dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell), aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey90", size = 0.2, stroke = 0) +
  geom_point(data = sub_umap, aes(colour = class), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = share_pal, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(title = "Where the sharing cells sit") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 11))

# Within-cell ratio: of a sharing cell's molecules that name one of the two sites, what share is
# IS01? A sub-clone carrying both predicts a spread around the detection-implied value, not a pile
# at the extremes.
ratio <- clip_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(match_sites %in% c("IS01", "IS02")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cell) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n1 = sum(match_sites == "IS01"), n2 = sum(match_sites == "IS02"),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::filter(n1 + n2 >= 2) |>
  dplyr::mutate(frac1 = n1 / (n1 + n2),
                class = ifelse(n1 > 0 & n2 > 0, "both sites", "one site only"))

p_ratio <- ggplot(ratio, aes(frac1, fill = class)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 9, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`both sites` = "#009E73", `one site only` = "grey70"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "share of the cell's molecules naming IS01", y = "cells",
       title = "Within-cell ratio, cells with \u2265 2 molecules") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 11))

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_umap, p_ratio, widths = c(2, 1))
```

**Read this as the weakest link in the finding rather than its confirmation.** The sharing cells are
too few to settle their own position — 20 of them across both tubes — so the UMAP panel can show
that they are not obviously a separate island, which is consistent with a sub-clone, and cannot show
that they form one. The ratio panel is the sharper of the two: a sub-clone carrying both proviruses
predicts a spread of ratios, while a doublet of two single-site cells predicts the extremes. What it
cannot do is distinguish a sub-clone from correlated detection within one clone, because both put
balanced ratios in deep cells.

So the structure remains open, exactly as stated above. This figure is here because the finding
should be inspectable, not because it closes it — and a cell-barcode-level DNA assay on sorted B0303
cells is what would.

**Verdict.** Doublets and ambient are excluded as the dominant mechanism, by a control that
survives the one objection that would have killed it. A **double-insertion sub-clone inside B0303**,
carrying IS01 and IS02 in perhaps a quarter to a third of its cells, is the reading that fits both
the cross-mouse contrast and the depth gradient; IS03's absence from every co-occurrence is
consistent with it. The original "multi-copy founders are absent" was wrong, and the "undetermined"
that replaced it was too weak.

What is still open is the structure, not the existence: how many founders B0303 holds, whether IS06
and IS08 belong to the same sub-clone, and how much of the shortfall against full sharing is a real
sub-clone fraction rather than residual correlated detection. The `ambiguous` flag stays as it is so
downstream work can decide for itself.

What the data *does* settle is **replicate separation**, and the genome-mapped channel sharpened it
considerably. Every site is mono-replicate — the dominant hashtag class accounts for 96–100% of each
site's called cells — and the sites divide three ways:

| replicate | sites | labelled cells |
|---|---|---|
| B0303 | IS01, IS02, IS03, IS06, IS07, IS08, IS13 | 819 |
| B0304 | IS05, IS10, IS11, IS12, IS14, IS15 | 197 |
| B0301 | IS04, IS09 | 197 |
| B0302 | none | 0 |

Sites in different animals are necessarily distinct founders, whatever the within-replicate structure
proves to be. The change from the previous run is B0304: it had exactly one site, and now it has six,
headed by IS10 at 99 cells. The seven B0303 sites remain unresolved against each other.

#### The other instrument, and why it does not decide this

There is a second way to measure assignment error, and it is tempting because it runs on real reads
rather than decoys: every site belongs to exactly one mouse and every cell's hashtag names its mouse,
so **a clip assigned to a site in the wrong mouse is a detectable error**. It needs the hashtag calls,
which live in the targets store rather than the pipeline's outputs, so it is computed here:

```{r mono-replicate}
# Every assignment-tier match, with the mouse of its site and the mouse of its cell. A landing in
# the wrong mouse is an error that real reads can show, at every clip length.
mono <- clip_site_matches(file.path(sites_dir, "work", "all_clips.fa"),
                          file.path(sites_dir, "work", "site_flanks.fa"), min_len = 1L) |>
  dplyr::filter(assign_keep(clip_len, nm, budget)) |>
  dplyr::semi_join(dplyr::select(sites, site_id), by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(site_replicate, site_id, site_mouse = mouse), by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::transmute(embedding, cell,
                                     cell_mouse = sub("^TotalSeq-", "", as.character(replicate))),
                    by = "cell") |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^B03", cell_mouse)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cross = cell_mouse != site_mouse,
                band = cut(clip_len, c(0, 9, 14, 19, 29, Inf),
                           labels = c("6–9", "10–14", "15–19", "20–29", "30+")))

dplyr::bind_rows(
  mono |> dplyr::group_by(band) |> dplyr::summarise(molecules = dplyr::n(),
            `cross-mouse` = sum(cross), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(band = as.character(band)),
  dplyr::tibble(band = "pooled", molecules = nrow(mono), `cross-mouse` = sum(mono$cross))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rate = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * `cross-mouse` / molecules)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

It passes at the current floor and it is reported for that. **It cannot set the floor**, for two
reasons that are structural rather than fixable by more data.

It measures chance matching *plus* hashtag misassignment *plus* doublets. Four of the seven
cross-mouse landings sit at 23, 27 and 45 bases, where an exact positional match to the wrong flank
is not a coincidence, so the confound floor is **0.48%** against a 1% tolerance. And the resulting
power at the band that matters — 94 molecules at 6–9 bp — is not close to sufficient:

| if the true clip error were | power to detect it |
|---|---|
| 1% | **8%** |
| 2% | 20% |
| 5% | 62% |
| 10% | 93% |

So it can exclude an error rate above ~5% and cannot certify one below 1%, which is the only decision
a floor needs. The decoys measure chance matching alone and can be cut in any number, so they have
the sample size this lacks. **Set the floor from decoys.**

**And do not read this curve's agreement as support for the floor** — it is consistent with almost
anything. The accepted set expects 0.31 spurious assignments in total, of which roughly 60% would
land in another mouse, so the expected cross-mouse count among the 96 molecules at 6–9 bp is about
**0.16**. Observing zero there is what you would see whether the floor were right or wrong. The
pooled improvement from 0.62% to 0.50% is not about the floor either: it happened because two of the
five rejected 10–12 bp assignments were themselves errors, which is the mismatch rule doing the work.
This control earns its place by being an independent check that *could* have objected, not by having
agreed. One detail worth recording either way: all seven
cross-mouse landings are on IS01 or IS02, the two largest clones, which is the prior-inflation
signature — ambiguous evidence drifting onto the biggest hypothesis — showing up even at the current
floor.
